title: Primitive, Composite, and Reference-Type Concepts
learningObjectives: Describe the broad idea of primitive or simple values.
Explain why composite values group related data together.
Recognize reference-based access to objects or composite structures.
Distinguish a value from a reference used to reach it.
Understand that exact type categories and copy behavior vary by language.

understand.concept: Many languages distinguish simple values from structures that combine multiple pieces of data. Primitive or basic values commonly represent one item such as a number, Boolean, or character. Composite values group fields or elements, such as arrays, records, objects, or tuples. Some composite values are accessed through references, meaning a variable may hold a way to reach shared data rather than an independent copy of that data.
understand.whyItMatters: This distinction affects how data is organized, passed to functions, copied, changed, and shared. It helps learners predict whether an update changes only one value or may be visible through another variable that refers to the same structure.
understand.analogy: A primitive value is like one label on a card. A composite structure is like a folder holding several labeled cards. A reference is like a locator pointing to a particular folder; copying the locator does not necessarily copy the folder.
understand.analogyLimit: Languages differ: some primitives are copied by value, some structures have value semantics, and some objects are reference-based. The analogy does not determine the behavior of a specific language.

explain.narrative: Simple values are useful when one independent fact is enough. Composite structures are useful when several related facts belong together or when a sequence of values must be managed. A reference can make it possible for multiple parts of a program to access one shared structure. Before assuming how assignment or function calls behave, consult the language's rules for that type. A type's name alone may not reveal its copying, mutability, or ownership behavior.

examples.title: A single simple value
examples.explanation: The variable holds one value representing age; numeric operations may be appropriate.

examples.title: A composite sequence
examples.explanation: The sequence groups multiple related values and supports indexed access or traversal.

examples.title: A grouped record
examples.explanation: The structure groups different fields that describe one entity.

examples.title: Two names reaching shared data
examples.code: let a = {count: 1}; let b = a; b.count = 2;
examples.explanation: In this JavaScript example, a and b refer to the same object, so reading a.count also sees 2.

examples.title: Independent primitive assignment
examples.code: let x = 7; let y = x; y = 9;
examples.explanation: Changing y's assigned primitive value does not change x.

commonMistakes: Assuming composite data is always copied automatically on assignment.
Assuming reference semantics are identical in every language.
Using a collection when a single value is enough or separate unrelated variables when a structure would be clearer.
Confusing a variable holding a reference with the object itself.
Mutating shared data without realizing other code may observe the change.

guidedTask.title: Guided: Choose and explain a representation
guidedTask.instructions: Use the lesson ideas to analyze the task "Primitive, Composite, and Reference-Type Concepts". For each case, identify the value(s), what they represent, and the operation or type behavior that matters.
steps: State what each data item represents in the real-world task.
Choose a representation and justify why it preserves the needed information.
Identify a valid operation and one operation that should be avoided or checked.
Describe one edge case or conversion risk.
Summarize what a learner should verify in the language they are using.
guidedTask.starterCode: // Write notes or a small example that demonstrates the lesson concept

independentTask.title: Independent: Data and type decision notes
independentTask.instructions: Create three examples from a simple application and explain the data representation choices.
requirements: Include one simple value and one composite value.
Explain the purpose of each representation.
Show one assignment or operation and predict its behavior.
Identify one likely mistake or boundary case.
Explain any language-specific rule you would verify rather than assume.

hints: Begin with the meaning of the value, not its appearance.
Ask whether arithmetic, ordering, formatting, or grouping is required.
Keep identifiers and quantities conceptually distinct.
Composite data groups related values; references may allow sharing.
Check the target language's actual assignment, conversion, and type-checking rules.
